```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false

library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(patchwork)
library(scales)
library(viridis)
library(ggeffects)
library(marginaleffects)
library(plotly)

systemfonts::register_font(
  "Albert Sans",
  plain  = "../../stylesheets/fonts/AlbertSans-400.ttf",
  bold   = "../../stylesheets/fonts/AlbertSans-700.ttf",
  italic = "../../stylesheets/fonts/AlbertSans-400.ttf"
)
knitr::opts_chunk$set(dev = "ragg_png", dev.args = list(bg = "white"))

penguins  <- read.csv("data/penguins.csv")
gapminder <- read.csv("data/gapminder.csv")
safi      <- read.csv("data/SAFI_clean.csv")
datasaurus <- read.delim("data/datasaurus.tsv")

uzk_blue      <- "#005176"
uzk_turquoise <- "#009dcc"
uzk_coral     <- "#ea564f"
uzk_muted     <- "#547685"

theme_set(
  theme_minimal(base_family = "Albert Sans", base_size = 15) +
    theme(
      panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
      plot.title.position = "plot",
      plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = rel(1.05)),
      plot.subtitle = element_text(colour = uzk_muted),
      plot.caption = element_text(colour = uzk_muted, size = rel(0.75)),
      legend.position = "bottom"
    )
)
```

## Overview {.smaller}

::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="56%"}
### Learning objectives

By the end of this session, you can:

1. **Control** scales, guides, limits, and coordinates deliberately.
2. **Explain** how stats and positions change what a geom represents.
3. **Plot** model predictions, slopes, and uncertainty with [`marginaleffects`](https://marginaleffects.com/) and [`ggeffects`](https://strengejacke.github.io/ggeffects/).
4. **Compose**, export, and audit a publication-ready figure.

### Session plan

- **Scales and coordinates:** transformations, limits versus zoom, guides — 15 min
- **Under the hood:** the plot object, statistics, positions — 15 min
- **Models and uncertainty:** intervals, predictions, slopes, interactions — 25 min
- **Publication:** themes, composition, export, accessibility, ecosystem — 15 min
- **Hands-on:** a model plot and a composite figure — 20 min

*Total: 90 minutes.*

:::

::: {.column width="44%"}

::: {.callout-note}
### This is the sequel

We assume you can build a plot with [`aes()`](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/reference/aes.html), `geom_*()`, and [`labs()`](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/reference/labs.html). The basic workshop is [`slides.qmd`](slides.html).
:::

**Prerequisites:** the basic workshop or equivalent experience with [`ggplot2`](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/).

**Materials:** [`slides-advanced.qmd`](https://github.com/SFB1252/talks/blob/main/docs/workshops/30-data-visualization-ggplot2/slides-advanced.qmd), [`scripts/ggplot2-advanced.R`](https://github.com/SFB1252/talks/blob/main/docs/workshops/30-data-visualization-ggplot2/scripts/ggplot2-advanced.R), and the [`data/` folder](https://github.com/SFB1252/talks/tree/main/docs/workshops/30-data-visualization-ggplot2/data).

**Basic deck:** [`slides.qmd`](slides.html) covers perception, the grammar, mappings, geoms, facets, colour, and integrity traps.
:::

:::

::: {.notes}
This deck assumes the basic vocabulary. Do not re-teach aes() and geom_*(); spend the time on the choices that change the statistical claim: scales, limits, statistics, positions, models, and composition. If time runs short, do the model plot and composition tasks only.
:::

---

## From the basic deck to this one {.smaller}

::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="52%"}
### You already have

- `data` → [`aes()`](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/reference/aes.html) → `geom_*()`
- `facet_*()`, `scale_*()`, [`labs()`](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/reference/labs.html), and a house theme
- the habit of plotting the data, not only the summary

### What changes here

1. **We stop accepting defaults** — scales, guides, limits, coordinates
2. **We look inside the object** — statistics, positions, rendering
3. **We plot models** — predictions, slopes, and named intervals
4. **We finish the figure** — composition, export, accessibility
:::

::: {.column width="48%"}
```r
# The basic vocabulary still applies
ggplot(penguins,
       aes(flipper_length_mm, body_mass_g,
           colour = species)) +
  geom_point() +
  facet_wrap(~ island) +
  scale_colour_viridis_d() +
  labs(x = "Flipper length (mm)",
       y = "Body mass (g)",
       colour = NULL)
```

::: {.callout-important}
### One sentence

The basic deck taught you to **build** a plot. This deck teaches you to **control** it — and to **defend** every choice in the caption.
:::
:::

:::

::: {.notes}
Use this slide as a checkpoint, not a re-teach. Ask for one example of a plot they built since the basic session. Then state the promise of the sequel: every default becomes a choice, and every choice becomes a claim you can defend.
:::

## Part I: Scales, guides, coordinates {.center}

### After this part: control the data-to-pixel mapping

---

## Transform before or after the stat {.smaller}

```{r}
#| label: plot-transform
#| fig-width: 9.6
#| fig-height: 3.6
#| fig-alt: "Two scatter plots of life expectancy against GDP per capita in 2007. Left: scale_x_log10(), where the fitted line is straight because the model was fitted to log GDP. Right: coord_trans(x = 'log10') with the same raw-scale linear model, which appears curved on the log axis."
g2007 <- gapminder |> filter(year == 2007)
dollar_k <- function(x) paste0("$", format(x / 1000, trim = TRUE, scientific = FALSE), "k")

life_y <- function() scale_y_continuous(limits = c(38, 92),
                                         breaks = seq(40, 90, 10))

p_scale <- ggplot(g2007, aes(gdpPercap, lifeExp)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5, colour = uzk_blue) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ x, se = FALSE,
              colour = uzk_coral, linewidth = 0.9) +
  scale_x_log10(breaks = c(1000, 3000, 10000, 30000), labels = dollar_k) +
  life_y() +
  labs(title = "scale_x_log10()",
       subtitle = "the model is fitted to log GDP: a straight line",
       x = "GDP per capita", y = "Life expectancy")

p_coord <- ggplot(g2007, aes(gdpPercap, lifeExp)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5, colour = uzk_blue) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ x, se = FALSE,
              colour = uzk_coral, linewidth = 0.9) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(1000, 3000, 10000, 30000), labels = dollar_k) +
  life_y() +
  coord_trans(x = "log10") +
  labs(title = 'coord_trans(x = "log10")',
       subtitle = "the same raw-scale model, warped by the axis",
       x = "GDP per capita", y = NULL)

p_scale | p_coord
```

::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="55%"}
### Where the transformation sits changes the model

- [`scale_x_log10()`](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/reference/scale_continuous.html) transforms the **data before the stat**: the smooth is fitted to log GDP
- [`coord_trans()`](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/reference/coord_transform.html) transforms the **plane after the stat**: the smooth is fitted to raw GDP and the axis warps the result
- Both panels plot life expectancy against income; only the left one is a log-linear model

Breaks and labels remain scale arguments in both cases. The scale form and the coordinate form are not interchangeable, even though the axes look similar.
:::

::: {.column width="45%"}
```r
# data transformed, then modelled
scale_x_log10()

# model on the raw scale,
# display transformed
coord_trans(x = "log10")
```

::: {.callout-important}
### The caption must name the model

"Life expectancy rises with income" means something different in the two panels: one is a log-linear relation, the other a linear one drawn on a log axis.
:::
:::

:::

::: {.notes}
Same data, same geom, same formula; only the placement of the log10 differs. On the left it acts before the smoother, so the model is linear in log GDP and the line is straight. On the right it acts after the smoother, so the model is linear in GDP and the line curves upward on screen. Ask which panel answers "does each doubling of income buy the same gain in life expectancy?" — the left one. This is the same mechanism as on the limits slide: a scale changes the data the stat sees; a coordinate changes only the view.
:::
---

## Limits are not zoom {.smaller}

```{r}
#| label: plot-limits
#| fig-width: 9.6
#| fig-height: 3.3
#| fig-alt: "Two scatter plots of body mass against bill length restricted to 40 to 50 millimetres: scale limits drop outlying data and change the fitted line, while coord_cartesian keeps all data and only zooms the view."
mass_y <- function() scale_y_continuous(
  limits = range(penguins$body_mass_g, na.rm = TRUE),
  breaks = c(3000, 4000, 5000, 6000))

p_base <- ggplot(penguins, aes(bill_length_mm, body_mass_g)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.35, colour = uzk_blue) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ x, se = FALSE,
              colour = uzk_coral, linewidth = 0.9) +
  mass_y()

p_crop <- p_base +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(40, 50)) +
  labs(title = "scale_x_continuous(limits = ...)",
       subtitle = "rows outside the limits are dropped")

p_zoom <- p_base +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(40, 50)) +
  labs(title = "coord_cartesian(xlim = ...)",
       subtitle = "all data are kept; the view is zoomed")

p_crop | p_zoom
```

::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="55%"}
- `scale_*_*(limits = ...)` **removes** data outside the limits, then computes the stat. Means, smooths, and summaries change.
- [`coord_cartesian(xlim = ...)`](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/reference/coord_cartesian.html) **zooms** the viewport. All data contribute to the stat; only the visible window changes.
:::

::: {.column width="45%"}
::: {.callout-warning}
### Never truncate a bar chart's baseline

Bars encode magnitude by **length from zero**. A truncated baseline violates proportional ink and exaggerates differences. Zooming is defensible for scatter plots and lines when the question is local — and when the caption says so.
:::

**Theory:** a coordinate system changes the **view**; a scale changes the **data-to-visual mapping**.
:::

:::

::: {.notes}
This is a subtle but important distinction. In the left panel the regression line is fitted only to the 40–50 mm subset, so the slope changes; in the right panel the line is fitted to all data and merely clipped. Ask which one answers "what is the relation in this range?" and which one answers "what is the overall relation?"
:::

## Coordinates {.smaller}

```{r}
#| label: plot-coord
#| fig-width: 9.6
#| fig-height: 3.4
#| fig-alt: "Pie chart and horizontal bar chart of the same penguin species counts; the bar chart makes differences easier to compare."
p_bar_pie <- penguins |> count(species) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = "", y = n, fill = species)) +
  geom_col(width = 1, colour = "white") +
  coord_polar(theta = "y") +
  labs(title = "Pie chart", x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme_void(base_family = "Albert Sans") +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom",
        plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", colour = uzk_blue))

p_bar_flat <- penguins |> count(species) |>
  ggplot(aes(n, species, fill = species)) +
  geom_col(show.legend = FALSE, width = 0.65) +
  labs(title = "Bar chart", x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

p_bar_pie | p_bar_flat
```

::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}
### The coordinate system is part of the grammar

- [`coord_cartesian()`](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/reference/coord_cartesian.html): default Cartesian plane; zoom and set limits
- [`coord_fixed(ratio = ...)`](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/reference/coord_fixed.html): lock the aspect ratio; essential for maps and shapes
- [`coord_flip()`](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/reference/coord_flip.html): swap axes (now usually replaced by mapping the discrete variable to *y*)
- [`coord_polar()`](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/reference/coord_radial.html): wrap a linear axis around a circle
- [`coord_radial()`](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/reference/coord_radial.html): modern radial coordinates with partial circles (ggplot2 ≥ 3.5.0)
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.callout-warning}
### A pie chart is a stacked bar in polar coordinates

Angle and area are less accurate than position and length [@cleveland1984graphical]. A pie works for a rough part-to-whole impression with two or three slices; it fails for precise comparison.

**Better:** a bar or dot plot, sorted by value, with direct labels.
:::

**Theory:** coordinates transform the **plane**, not the data. The same geoms can be arranged in a space that helps or hinders decoding.
:::

:::

::: {.notes}
The pie and bar show exactly the same counts. The bar is easier to compare because the bars share a common baseline and a common scale. If a pie is required by a journal or stakeholder, keep it to a few slices, order them, and label directly.
:::

---

## Guides and legends {.smaller}

::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="48%"}
### A guide is the inverse of a scale

Axes, legends, and colourbars let the reader recover the data values from the plotted geoms.

- [`guides(colour = "none")`](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/reference/guides.html) removes a guide but keeps the scale
- [`guide_legend(nrow = 1, override.aes = list(size = 3))`](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/reference/guide_legend.html) controls the keys
- [`guide_axis(angle = 45)`](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/reference/guide_axis.html) handles crowded labels
- [`theme(legend.position = "top")`](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/reference/theme.html) moves the legend; [`guides()`](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/reference/guides.html) controls its content
- direct labels often beat a legend, especially for few groups

**Rule:** if the legend repeats information the reader can see on the geoms, replace it with a direct label.
:::

::: {.column width="52%"}
```{r}
#| label: plot-guides
#| fig-width: 5.4
#| fig-height: 6.4
#| fig-alt: "Two bar charts of penguin counts by species: the top uses a colour legend, the bottom removes the legend and labels each bar with its count."
counts <- penguins |> count(species)

p_leg <- ggplot(counts, aes(species, n, fill = species)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.65) +
  scale_fill_viridis_d(end = 0.85, name = NULL) +
  labs(title = "Legend", x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")

p_dir <- ggplot(counts, aes(species, n, fill = species)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.65, show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_text(aes(label = n), vjust = -0.4, size = 3.4) +
  scale_fill_viridis_d(end = 0.85, guide = "none") +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.14))) +
  labs(title = "Direct labels", x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

p_leg / p_dir
```
:::

:::

::: {.notes}
The two panels show the same counts. The top uses a legend; the bottom removes it and labels the values directly. Removing a guide is not the same as removing a scale: the fill scale still exists, it simply has no reader-facing key. Use guides() when you want to keep the scale but change or suppress its guide.
:::

## Part II: The object, stats, positions {.center}

### After this part: explain what a geom represents

---

## A plot is a specification {.smaller}

::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="52%"}
### Nothing is drawn until it is rendered

```r
p <- ggplot(penguins,
            aes(flipper_length_mm, body_mass_g)) +
  geom_point()

class(p)                 # "gg" "ggplot"
length(p$layers)         # 1
p                        # renders now
ggplot_build(p)$data[[1]] # computed values
```

A [`ggplot`](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/reference/ggplot.html) object is a **list of specifications**. Building it does not draw pixels.

Consequences:

- layers can be added, removed, reused, and composed
- [`ggsave()`](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/reference/ggsave.html) renders without displaying
- [`ggplot_build()`](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/reference/ggplot_build.html) exposes the output of stats and scales
- functions can return plots; loops and [`purrr::map()`](https://purrr.tidyverse.org/reference/map.html) work
- Quarto renders the object at the point where it is printed

:::

::: {.column width="48%"}
### Why this matters for theory

The separation of **specification** from **rendering** mirrors the grammar:

1. declare the data and the mapping
2. declare the transformation
3. declare the scales and coordinates
4. render

This is also why debugging is possible: a wrong plot is usually a wrong *specification*, not a drawing bug.

::: {.callout-tip}
### Inspect the pipeline

`ggplot_build(p)$data` shows what the stats computed; [`ggplot_gtable()`](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/reference/ggplot_gtable.html) shows the rendered grobs. Use them when a plot looks wrong and you cannot tell which layer is responsible.
:::
:::

:::

::: {.notes}
This slide is the bridge from theory to practice. Emphasise that `p` is an object, not a side effect. If someone is used to base R, this is the conceptual shift: you describe the plot, then print it.
:::

---

## Statistical transformations {.smaller}

::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="52%"}
### A stat computes a new data frame

Every geom has a default stat; every stat has a default geom.

| Geom | Default stat | Computed variables |
|---|---|---|
| [`geom_bar`](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/reference/geom_bar.html) | [`stat_count`](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/reference/geom_bar.html) | `count`, `prop` |
| [`geom_histogram`](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/reference/geom_histogram.html) | [`stat_bin`](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/reference/geom_histogram.html) | `count`, `density` |
| [`geom_boxplot`](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/reference/geom_boxplot.html) | [`stat_boxplot`](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/reference/geom_boxplot.html) | `ymin`, `lower`, `middle`, `upper`, `ymax`, `outliers` |
| [`geom_smooth`](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/reference/geom_smooth.html) | [`stat_smooth`](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/reference/geom_smooth.html) | `y`, `ymin`, `ymax`, `se` |
| [`geom_density`](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/reference/geom_density.html) | [`stat_density`](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/reference/geom_density.html) | `density`, `count`, `scaled` |

[`stat_ecdf()`](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/reference/stat_ecdf.html) has no `geom_ecdf()`: its default geom is [`geom_step()`](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/reference/geom_path.html).

[`after_stat()`](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/reference/aes_eval.html) maps a **computed** variable; `..count..` is the older syntax.

:::

::: {.column width="48%"}
```r
# counts (default)
ggplot(diamonds, aes(cut)) +
  geom_bar()

# proportions, computed by the stat
ggplot(diamonds, aes(cut)) +
  geom_bar(aes(y = after_stat(prop),
               group = 1))

# identity: the data already contain y
penguins |>
  count(species) |>
  ggplot(aes(species, n)) +
  geom_col()
```

```{r}
#| label: plot-stat
#| fig-width: 4.4
#| fig-height: 3.2
#| fig-alt: "Bar chart of diamond counts by cut, from Fair to Ideal, produced by geom_bar() without a y variable."
ggplot(diamonds, aes(cut)) +
  geom_bar(fill = uzk_blue) +
  scale_x_discrete(labels = function(x) gsub(" ", "\n", x)) +
  labs(x = "Cut", y = "Count",
       title = "geom_bar() computes counts",
       subtitle = "stat_count(); no y supplied")
```

**Theory:** statistics are **first-class** plot components. A bar chart of counts is a statistical claim, not a raw data display.
:::

:::

::: {.notes}
This is where the grammar pays off: `geom_bar()` vs `geom_col()` is not a quirky naming detail, it is `stat_count()` vs `stat_identity()`. If you supply y, you probably want `geom_col()`. If you want proportions, let the stat compute them rather than pre-summarising by hand.
:::

---

## Positions for points: jitter and jitterdodge {.smaller}

```{r}
#| label: plot-jitter
#| fig-width: 9.6
#| fig-height: 4.4
#| fig-alt: "Two scatter plots of body mass by species and sex. Left, position_jitter() spreads the points but female and male observations still overlap; right, position_jitterdodge() spreads and separates the sexes within each species."
pos_data <- penguins |> filter(!is.na(sex), !is.na(body_mass_g))

p_jitter <- ggplot(pos_data, aes(species, body_mass_g, colour = sex)) +
  geom_point(position = position_jitter(width = 0.15, height = 0, seed = 1),
             alpha = 0.5, size = 1.8) +
  labs(title = "position_jitter()",
       subtitle = "spread, but the sexes still mix", x = NULL, y = "Body mass (g)")

p_jd <- ggplot(pos_data, aes(species, body_mass_g, colour = sex)) +
  geom_point(position = position_jitterdodge(jitter.width = 0.12,
                                             dodge.width = 0.75,
                                             seed = 1),
             alpha = 0.5, size = 1.8) +
  labs(title = "position_jitterdodge()",
       subtitle = "jitter inside each dodge slot", x = NULL, y = NULL)

(p_jitter | p_jd) +
  plot_layout(guides = "collect")
```

::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="52%"}
### Positions also apply to points

- [`position_jitter(width, height)`](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/reference/position_jitter.html): spreads coincident points
- [`position_jitterdodge()`](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/reference/position_jitterdodge.html): jitter **inside** dodged groups — the standard for paired groups
- `seed` fixes the layout, so the figure is reproducible
:::

::: {.column width="48%"}
- [`position_dodge2(preserve = "single")`](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/reference/position_dodge.html): dodges boxes and violins and closes gaps left by absent groups
- [`geom_jitter()`](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/reference/geom_jitter.html) is [`geom_point(position = "jitter")`](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/reference/geom_point.html), with the same caveats
- positions run **after** the stat: counts and fits are unchanged, only the points move

:::

:::

::: {.notes}
The left panel spreads the points, but the colour groups still overlap, so the eye cannot compare the sexes within a species. The right panel separates the sexes and keeps the spread. The seed argument matters: without it, every render scrambles the points, which breaks reproducibility of the figure. The basic deck showed identity, dodge, stack, and fill for bars; here the same machinery is applied to points, where it is needed more often.
:::

## Part III: Models and uncertainty {.center}

### After this part: plot a model and name its interval

---

## What error bars actually mean {.smaller}

::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="45%"}
### Five different intervals

| Quantity | What it describes | Typical use |
|---|---|---|
| **SD** | spread of observations | reference range, prediction |
| **SE** | precision of an estimated mean | error bar around a mean |
| **95% CI** | repeated-sampling coverage of a parameter | inference about a mean or effect |
| **95% CrI** | posterior probability of a parameter | Bayesian inference |
| **PI** | spread of future observations | prediction, not estimation |

::: {.callout-warning}
An error bar without a label is not information. "Mean ± SE" and "mean ± SD" can differ by a factor of $\sqrt{n}$.
:::

**Theory:** an interval is a claim about a **target**: the data (SD, PI) or an estimate of the mean (SE, CI, CrI).
:::

::: {.column width="55%"}
```{r}
#| label: plot-intervals
#| fig-width: 5.8
#| fig-height: 3.3
#| fig-alt: "Five horizontal intervals for the same sample mean body mass of 4,202 grams. The 95 percent prediction interval is widest, then the standard deviation; the standard error, 95 percent confidence interval and 95 percent credible interval are narrow around the mean. With a flat prior the credible interval coincides with the confidence interval."
mass <- penguins$body_mass_g[!is.na(penguins$body_mass_g)]
n <- length(mass)
m <- mean(mass)
s <- sd(mass)
se <- s / sqrt(n)
tcrit <- qt(0.975, n - 1)

intervals <- data.frame(
  interval = factor(c("SE", "95% CrI", "95% CI", "SD", "95% PI"),
                    levels = c("SE", "95% CrI", "95% CI", "SD", "95% PI")),
  lo = c(m - se, m - tcrit * se, m - tcrit * se, m - s,
         m - tcrit * s * sqrt(1 + 1 / n)),
  hi = c(m + se, m + tcrit * se, m + tcrit * se, m + s,
         m + tcrit * s * sqrt(1 + 1 / n)),
  target = c("estimate", "estimate", "estimate", "data", "data"))

ggplot(intervals, aes(y = interval, colour = target)) +
  geom_segment(aes(x = lo, xend = hi, yend = interval), linewidth = 1.8) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = m, linetype = 2, colour = uzk_muted) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(data = uzk_muted, estimate = uzk_coral),
                      guide = "none") +
  labs(title = "Same mean, five intervals",
       subtitle = "flat prior: the CrI and CI coincide",
       x = "Body mass (g)", y = NULL)
```

The grey intervals describe **observations**; the coral ones describe the **mean**.
:::

:::

::: {.notes}
The key distinction is target, not formula. Two intervals computed from the same data can differ by an order of magnitude because they answer different questions. The SD and PI describe where observations fall; the SE, CI and CrI describe where the mean is. Point out that with a flat prior the CrI and CI coincide numerically — the Bayesian and frequentist statements differ in meaning, not in this number. Many published error bars are unlabelled, which makes them uninterpretable.
:::

---

## The trap: the wrong target {.smaller}

```{r}
#| label: plot-within
#| fig-width: 9.6
#| fig-height: 3.6
#| fig-alt: "Three panels. Left: mean extra sleep for two groups with between-subject 95 percent confidence intervals, which overlap. Middle: one line per participant joining their Group 1 and Group 2 values, nine of ten rising. Right: the ten paired differences per participant, with a 95 percent confidence interval from 0.7 to 2.5 hours that excludes zero."
sleep_means <- sleep |>
  group_by(group) |>
  summarise(m = mean(extra), se = sd(extra) / sqrt(n()), n = n(),
            .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(lo = m - qt(0.975, n - 1) * se,
         hi = m + qt(0.975, n - 1) * se)

p_between <- ggplot(sleep_means, aes(group, m, colour = group)) +
  geom_point(size = 2.6) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi), width = 0.12, linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = 2, colour = uzk_muted) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(uzk_blue, uzk_coral), guide = "none") +
  scale_x_discrete(labels = c("Group 1", "Group 2")) +
  labs(title = "Between-subject 95% CIs",
       subtitle = "the two intervals overlap",
       x = NULL, y = "Extra sleep (hours)")

participant_lines <- sleep |>
  arrange(ID, group) |>
  group_by(ID) |>
  mutate(rises = extra[2] > extra[1]) |>
  ungroup()

p_participants <- ggplot(participant_lines,
                         aes(group, extra, group = ID, colour = rises)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.7) +
  geom_point(size = 1.7) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = uzk_coral, `FALSE` = uzk_muted),
                      guide = "none") +
  scale_x_discrete(labels = c("Group 1", "Group 2")) +
  labs(title = "By participant", subtitle = "nine of ten lines rise",
       x = NULL, y = NULL)

paired <- sleep |>
  pivot_wider(id_cols = ID, names_from = group, values_from = extra,
              names_prefix = "g") |>
  mutate(diff = g2 - g1)

diff_mean <- mean(paired$diff)
diff_ci <- qt(0.975, nrow(paired) - 1) * sd(paired$diff) / sqrt(nrow(paired))

p_within <- ggplot(paired, aes(1, diff)) +
  geom_rect(aes(xmin = 0.85, xmax = 1.15,
                ymin = diff_mean - diff_ci, ymax = diff_mean + diff_ci),
            fill = uzk_coral, alpha = 0.22, inherit.aes = FALSE) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = 2, colour = uzk_muted) +
  geom_point(size = 1.9, alpha = 0.75, colour = uzk_blue) +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0.7, 1.3)) +
  labs(title = "Paired differences", subtitle = "the 95% CI excludes zero",
       x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_blank())

p_between | p_participants | p_within
```

::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="55%"}
### Within-subject data need within-subject intervals

Between-subject CIs are too wide when the same participants contribute to every condition: they include stable individual differences, which the question does not ask about. In the sleep data the two group intervals overlap, yet every participant but one slept longer in Group 2.

- normalise per participant, then compute the CI [@morey2008confidence]
- bootstrap **participants**, not observations
- plot **by-participant** effects or paired differences
- use a multilevel model and plot its predictions
:::

::: {.column width="45%"}
**Default trap:** [`stat_summary(fun.data = mean_se)`](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/reference/stat_summary.html) is between-subject.

**Preferred:** [`plot_predictions(fit, condition = "condition")`](https://rdrr.io/cran/marginaleffects/man/plot_predictions.html).

::: {.callout-tip}
When *N* is small, show every observation. A mean and an error bar can hide a bimodal or skewed distribution.
:::
:::

:::

::: {.notes}
The sleep dataset is paired: ten participants, each measured in both groups. The left panel shows the default — group means with between-subject confidence intervals — and the intervals overlap, which invites the conclusion that there is no effect. The middle panel shows every participant's pair of values; the lines make the consistent rise visible before any summary. The right panel shows the within-subject differences: nine of ten are positive and the CI excludes zero. The between-subject interval is not wrong, it answers a different question. For within-subject designs, the default `mean_se` is between-subject and therefore conservative; normalise, plot paired differences, or fit a model and plot its predictions.
:::

---

## Model-based visualization {.smaller}

```{r}
#| label: plot-model
#| fig-width: 9.6
#| fig-height: 3.9
#| fig-alt: "Two panels showing the same penguin data as grey points with 95 percent confidence ribbons. Left: marginaleffects avg_predictions(), averaged over the sample, with the three species curves sitting about 260 grams lower. Right: ggeffects ggpredict(), holding sex at its mode. Both show non-parallel species curves, an interaction on this scale."
fit <- lm(body_mass_g ~ flipper_length_mm * species + sex, data = penguins)
mass_scale <- function() scale_y_continuous(limits = c(2600, 6400))
raw_points <- function() geom_point(
  data = penguins, aes(flipper_length_mm, body_mass_g),
  colour = "grey65", alpha = 0.25, size = 0.6, inherit.aes = FALSE)

pred_mfx <- avg_predictions(fit, variables = c("flipper_length_mm", "species"))
pred_mfx$species <- factor(pred_mfx$species,
                           levels = c("Adelie", "Chinstrap", "Gentoo"))

p_mfx <- ggplot(pred_mfx, aes(flipper_length_mm, estimate,
                              colour = species, fill = species)) +
  raw_points() +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = conf.low, ymax = conf.high), alpha = 0.18,
              colour = NA) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) +
  mass_scale() +
  labs(title = "marginaleffects: avg_predictions()",
       subtitle = "averaged over the sample: the sex mix",
       x = "Flipper length (mm)", y = "Body mass (g)",
       colour = NULL, fill = NULL)

pred_gg <- as.data.frame(
  ggeffects::ggpredict(fit, terms = c("flipper_length_mm", "species"))
)
pred_gg$group <- factor(pred_gg$group,
                        levels = c("Adelie", "Chinstrap", "Gentoo"))

p_gg <- ggplot(pred_gg, aes(x, predicted, colour = group, fill = group)) +
  raw_points() +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = conf.low, ymax = conf.high), alpha = 0.18,
              colour = NA) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) +
  mass_scale() +
  labs(title = "ggeffects: ggpredict()",
       subtitle = "typical values: sex held at its mode",
       x = "Flipper length (mm)", y = NULL,
       colour = NULL, fill = NULL)

(p_mfx | p_gg) +
  plot_layout(guides = "collect") &
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="56%"}
### Same model, two questions

Both panels come from `lm(body_mass_g ~ flipper_length_mm * species + sex)` and share the same y scale. The ~260 g gap is **sex**, the predictor neither panel conditions on:

- [`avg_predictions()`](https://rdrr.io/cran/marginaleffects/man/predictions.html) averages over the observed sample: every participant contributes
- [`ggpredict()`](https://strengejacke.github.io/ggeffects/reference/ggpredict.html) reports typical values: sex is held at its mode (male)
- both can do either — `datagrid(sex = "female")` versus `newdata = "average"`, and `condition = list(sex = "female")` versus `ggaverage()`

Non-parallel lines mean the interaction is present **on this scale**; the caption must name the scale and the setting.
:::

::: {.column width="44%"}
::: {.callout-important}
### Name the interval

- **CI for the mean:** narrower; "where is the average?"
- **PI for an observation:** wider; "where will a new case fall?"
- **CrI:** a posterior statement, not repeated sampling

`geom_smooth(se = TRUE)` gives a CI for the mean, not a prediction interval.
:::

**Preferred for models:** [`plot_predictions()`](https://rdrr.io/cran/marginaleffects/man/plot_predictions.html) for levels, [`plot_slopes()`](https://rdrr.io/cran/marginaleffects/man/plot_slopes.html) for rates.
:::

:::

::: {.notes}
Measured at 190 mm for Adelie: the sample-averaged prediction is 3,707 g, the typical-value prediction 3,965 g. The gap is the sex effect (522 g) times the share of females, so it is real and predictable. Two lessons: the two packages agree when asked the same question — `plot_predictions()` uses typical values and matches `ggpredict()` — and they answer different questions when one averages. Say in the caption whether the curves are averaged or held at typical values, and whether the interval is for the mean or for an observation. `avg_predictions()` is the averaging counterpart in marginaleffects; `plot_predictions()` is the typical-values one.
:::

## Part IV: Composition and publication {.center}

### After this part: assemble, export, and audit a figure

---

## Themes change the non-data ink {.smaller}

```{r}
#| label: plot-themes
#| fig-width: 9.6
#| fig-height: 3.3
#| fig-alt: "Four versions of the same scatter plot under theme_minimal, theme_bw, theme_classic, and theme_dark, showing how non-data ink changes while the data stay the same."
p_theme <- ggplot(penguins, aes(bill_length_mm, body_mass_g,
                                colour = species)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7, size = 1.8) +
  labs(title = "Same data, four themes", x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

th_min <- p_theme + theme_minimal(base_family = "Albert Sans", base_size = 12)
th_bw <- p_theme + theme_bw(base_family = "Albert Sans", base_size = 12)
th_classic <- p_theme + theme_classic(base_family = "Albert Sans", base_size = 12)
th_dark <- p_theme + theme_dark(base_family = "Albert Sans", base_size = 12)

(th_min | th_bw) / (th_classic | th_dark)
```

::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="52%"}
### The theme is a separate layer

- [`theme_minimal()`](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/reference/ggtheme.html), [`theme_bw()`](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/reference/ggtheme.html), [`theme_classic()`](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/reference/ggtheme.html), [`theme_void()`](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/reference/ggtheme.html)
- [`theme_set()`](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/reference/get_theme.html) changes the default for the session
- [`theme()`](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/reference/theme.html) overrides one element on one plot
- elements form a hierarchy: `plot.title`, `axis.text`, `panel.grid`, `legend.position`

The theme changes **non-data ink**, not the data or the statistical claim.
:::

::: {.column width="48%"}
```r
theme_uzk <- function(base_size = 15) {
  theme_minimal(base_family = "Albert Sans",
                base_size = base_size) +
    theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
          legend.position = "bottom")
}
theme_set(theme_uzk())
```

::: {.callout-tip}
Write a **house theme** once. Reuse it in every figure. Consistency is a form of reproducibility.
:::
:::

:::

::: {.notes}
Themes do not change the data or the statistical claim; they change readability. The dark theme is included only to show that a theme can invert the figure-ground relationship. For publication, prefer a light background with restrained gridlines and direct labels.
:::

---

## Composition: multiple panels, one figure {.smaller}

::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="58%"}
```{r}
#| label: plot-composition
#| fig-width: 8.8
#| fig-height: 4.6
#| fig-alt: "Four-panel composite figure labelled A to D showing the penguin body-mass distribution, boxplots by species, the flipper-to-mass relationship, and species composition by island, with one shared species legend at the bottom."
p_a <- ggplot(penguins, aes(body_mass_g, fill = species)) +
  geom_density(alpha = 0.4, colour = NA, show.legend = FALSE) +
  labs(title = "Distribution", x = NULL, y = NULL)

p_b <- ggplot(penguins, aes(species, body_mass_g, fill = species)) +
  geom_boxplot(show.legend = FALSE, alpha = 0.8) +
  labs(title = "Quantiles", x = NULL, y = NULL)

p_c <- ggplot(penguins, aes(flipper_length_mm, body_mass_g,
                            colour = species)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7, size = 1.5) +
  labs(title = "Relationship", x = NULL, y = NULL)

p_d <- penguins |> count(island, species) |>
  ggplot(aes(island, n, fill = species)) +
  geom_col(position = "fill", show.legend = FALSE) +
  labs(title = "Composition", x = NULL, y = NULL)

(p_a | p_b) / (p_c | p_d) +
  plot_annotation(tag_levels = "A") +
  plot_layout(guides = "collect") &
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

:::

::: {.column width="42%"}
### The figure is a layout, too

[`patchwork`](https://patchwork.data-imaginist.com/) composes ggplot objects with operators: `p1 + p2`, `p1 | p2`, `p1 / p2`, `(p1 | p2) / p3`.

```r
(p1 | p2) / (p3 | p4) +
  plot_annotation(
    tag_levels = "A",
    title = "A composite figure"
  ) +
  plot_layout(
    guides = "collect",
    widths = c(1, 1),
    heights = c(1, 1)
  )
```

- [`plot_layout(guides = "collect")`](https://patchwork.data-imaginist.com/reference/plot_layout.html): collects the panels' guides into one legend row; identical guides merge
- `& theme(...)`: apply a theme to every panel
- `cowplot::plot_grid()` and `ggdraw()` are alternatives, especially for insets
- compose panels only when they answer **one** question
:::

:::

::: {.notes}
The four panels show four different views of the same data. Tags A–D let the caption refer to panels. Patchwork cannot merge a colour guide (points) with a fill guide (bars), so panel D's legend is suppressed and its bar colours are read from panel C's key; `guides = "collect"` then centres the single legend. If the panels need different themes or scales, check whether they belong in the same figure at all.
:::

---

## Export without losing the plot {.smaller}

::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="52%"}
### Save at the final size

```r
ggsave(
  filename = "figures/penguins-mass.png",
  plot = p_first,
  width = 16, height = 10, units = "cm",
  dpi = 300,
  bg = "white",
  device = ragg::agg_png
)
```

- `width`, `height`, `units`: the **printed** dimensions
- `dpi = 300` (or 600) for raster; vector formats ignore dpi
- `bg = "white"` avoids transparent backgrounds in Word
- pass `plot =` explicitly in scripts; the default is the last plot
- [`ragg::agg_png`](https://ragg.r-lib.org/reference/agg_png.html) gives better text and anti-aliasing than the default PNG device
- [`svglite::svglite`](https://svglite.r-lib.org/reference/svglite.html) for SVG; `cairo_pdf` for PDF with embedded fonts
- **design at final size:** do not export large and shrink in Word
:::

::: {.column width="48%"}
### Format choice

| Format | Use for | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| PDF | journal submission, vector | fonts must be embedded |
| SVG | web, editable vector | good browser support |
| PNG | slides, web, raster images | 300–600 dpi |
| TIFF | journal requirements | often LZW compression |
| EPS | legacy workflows | avoid for new work |

### A pre-export checklist

- [ ] final dimensions and resolution
- [ ] fonts embedded or outlined
- [ ] colour profile (RGB or CMYK)
- [ ] text readable at 100%; grayscale check
- [ ] caption names *N*, interval, and source
- [ ] meaningful, versioned file name
:::

:::

::: {.notes}
The most common export problem is not resolution but sizing: a figure designed at 20 cm wide and shrunk to 8 cm has unreadable labels. Design at the final size. For journals, check whether they require vector or raster, RGB or CMYK, and embedded fonts. Keep the code that produced the figure, not just the figure.
:::

---

## Accessibility and integrity checklist {.smaller}

::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}
### Before you plot

- [ ] What is the **question**?
- [ ] What is the **unit** of observation?
- [ ] Which variables are **encoded**, and how?
- [ ] Is the **scale** common and honest?
- [ ] Are **raw data** and **uncertainty** shown?

### Colour and perception

- [ ] Colour-vision-deficiency safe; sufficient contrast
- [ ] Colour is not the **only** encoding
- [ ] Sequential, diverging, and qualitative palettes used correctly
- [ ] Print in grayscale still works

:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
### Text and context

- [ ] Direct labels and units where possible
- [ ] Readable font size at final size
- [ ] Caption states *N*, interval, and source
- [ ] Alt text for the web

### Integrity

- [ ] Bars start at zero
- [ ] No dual axes without a strong justification
- [ ] No 3-D distortion or chartjunk
- [ ] No causal overclaim; code and data available

::: {.callout-important}
**The test:** can a reader who missed the talk understand the figure — including what is uncertain — without asking you?
:::
:::

:::

::: {.notes}
This checklist is deliberately long; nobody applies all of it to every exploratory plot. Use the first column for analysis and the full list for publication. The final test is comprehension without the talk.
:::

---

## When interactivity helps {.smaller}

::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}
### A dense cloud: hover to read a point

```{r}
#| label: plotly-overplot
set.seed(42)
diamonds_small <- diamonds[sample(nrow(diamonds), 12000), ]

p_dense <- ggplot(diamonds_small,
                  aes(carat, price,
                      text = paste0("Carat: ", carat,
                                    "<br>Price: $", format(price, big.mark = ",")))) +
  geom_point(colour = uzk_blue, alpha = 0.35, size = 0.6) +
  labs(x = "Carat", y = "Price (USD)")

ggplotly(p_dense, tooltip = "text", width = 460, height = 300) |>
  config(displayModeBar = FALSE, scrollZoom = FALSE)
```
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
### A log scale: read exact values

```{r}
#| label: plotly-gapminder
g2007 <- gapminder |> filter(year == 2007)

p_gdp <- ggplot(g2007,
                aes(gdpPercap, lifeExp, size = pop, colour = continent,
                    text = paste0(country, " · ", continent,
                                  "<br>GDP per capita: $", round(gdpPercap),
                                  "<br>Life expectancy: ", round(lifeExp, 1)))) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.85) +
  scale_x_log10(labels = scales::label_dollar(scale = 1/1000, suffix = "k",
                                              accuracy = 1)) +
  scale_size_area(max_size = 7, guide = "none") +
  theme(legend.position = "none") +
  labs(x = "GDP per capita", y = "Life expectancy")

ggplotly(p_gdp, tooltip = "text", width = 460, height = 300) |>
  config(displayModeBar = FALSE, scrollZoom = FALSE)
```
:::

:::

::: {.callout-warning}
### What interactivity costs

- **Size:** plotly.js is embedded once (3.6 MB here), plus 0.6 MB of figure data for the diamonds
- **Print:** widgets vanish from PDF and handout exports
- **Alt text:** `fig-alt` does not reach a widget; screen readers get far less than from a static figure with a caption
- **Navigation:** hover and drag compete with the slide controls; disable the mode bar and scroll zoom, and never make a click part of the talk
:::

::: {.notes}
Hover a point in the dense cloud to read carat and price, then drag a box around the 1–2 carat band to zoom. The same question — where is the mass? — is answered statically by alpha, binning, or faceting; interactivity adds reading of individual values. The gapminder panel shows the other gain: a log axis makes exact values hard to read, and a tooltip fixes that. Both are exploration tools, not headline figures. If a figure must print, fall back to the static versions. Watch the deck size when you build: this slide embeds plotly.js once.
:::

---

## The ecosystem {.smaller}

::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}
### Core and scales

- [**ggplot2**](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/) — grammar, geoms, scales, themes
- [**scales**](https://scales.r-lib.org/) — breaks, labels, transformations
- [**viridis**](https://sjmgarnier.github.io/viridis/) — perceptually uniform palettes
- [**colorspace**](https://colorspace.r-forge.r-project.org/) — HCL colour spaces, CVD checks

### Distributions and uncertainty

- [**ggdist**](https://mjskay.github.io/ggdist/) — half-eye, dot, gradient, and interval geoms [@kay2024ggdist]
- [**ggridges**](https://wilkelab.org/ggridges/) — ridgeline plots
- [**bayesplot**](https://mc-stan.org/bayesplot/) — posterior diagnostics
- [**ggeffects**](https://strengejacke.github.io/ggeffects/) — tidy marginal predictions [@ludecke2018ggeffects]
- [**marginaleffects**](https://marginaleffects.com/) — predictions, slopes, comparisons [@arel2024marginaleffects]

:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
### Composition and annotation

- [**patchwork**](https://patchwork.data-imaginist.com/) — compose and align panels
- [**cowplot**](https://wilkelab.org/cowplot/) — grids, insets, annotations
- [**ggrepel**](https://ggrepel.slowkow.com/) — non-overlapping labels
- [**ggtext**](https://wilkelab.org/ggtext/) — rich text and markdown in labels

### Data, maps, and interaction

- [**sf**](https://r-spatial.github.io/sf/) — simple features and maps
- [**ggraph**](https://ggraph.data-imaginist.com/) — networks and trees
- [**plotly**](https://plotly.com/r/) — interactive HTML plots
- [**gt**](https://gt.rstudio.com/) — publication tables

::: {.callout-tip}
Browse the [ggplot2 extension gallery](https://exts.ggplot2.tidyverse.org/gallery/) before writing a new geom. Someone has probably solved your problem.
:::
:::

:::

::: {.notes}
Do not install everything. Start with ggplot2 + scales + patchwork + one uncertainty package. Add an extension when the grammar cannot express the geom you need. Check maintenance status and whether the extension is on CRAN.
:::

---

## Hands-on: model, compose, export {.smaller}

::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="55%"}
### 20 minutes, in pairs

Use [`data/penguins.csv`](https://github.com/SFB1252/talks/blob/main/docs/workshops/30-data-visualization-ggplot2/data/penguins.csv).

1. **Fit** `lm(body_mass_g ~ flipper_length_mm * species)` and plot predictions. Does the interaction change the interpretation?
2. **Plot slopes** with [`plot_slopes()`](https://rdrr.io/cran/marginaleffects/man/plot_slopes.html). Which group has the steepest relation?
3. **Compose** two panels with [`patchwork`](https://patchwork.data-imaginist.com/) and collect the legend.
4. **Export** at 16 × 10 cm, 300 dpi. Is the text readable at final size?
5. **Audit** the figure: is the interval a CI or a PI? Is colour the only encoding?

::: {.callout-tip}
### Hints

- [`plot_predictions(fit, condition = c("flipper_length_mm", "species"))`](https://rdrr.io/cran/marginaleffects/man/plot_predictions.html)
- [`plot_slopes(fit, variables = "flipper_length_mm", condition = "species")`](https://rdrr.io/cran/marginaleffects/man/plot_slopes.html)
- `(p1 | p2) + plot_layout(guides = "collect")`
- [`ggsave(..., width = 16, height = 10, units = "cm", dpi = 300)`](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/reference/ggsave.html)
:::
:::

::: {.column width="45%"}
### Starter code

```r
library(ggplot2)
library(patchwork)
library(marginaleffects)
penguins <- read.csv("data/penguins.csv")

fit <- lm(body_mass_g ~ flipper_length_mm * species,
          data = penguins)

p1 <- plot_predictions(fit,
  condition = c("flipper_length_mm", "species"))
p2 <- plot_slopes(fit,
  variables = "flipper_length_mm", condition = "species")

(p1 | p2) + plot_layout(guides = "collect")

ggsave("figure.png", width = 16, height = 10,
       units = "cm", dpi = 300)
```

::: {.callout-note}
Write the caption: what is the interval, what is the scale, and what would change if the model were wrong?
:::
:::

:::

::: {.notes}
If time is short, do tasks 1 and 3. The common errors here are a confidence band described as a prediction interval, a slope on the link scale interpreted on the response scale, and a composite figure whose panels answer different questions.
:::

---

## Five takeaways {.smaller}

::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="55%"}
### What to remember

1. **Scales are functions.** Transformations change the data seen by the stat; limits remove data; coordinates only zoom.
2. **The object is a specification.** Separating building from rendering makes plots composable and debuggable.
3. **Stats and positions define the geom.** [`geom_bar()`](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/reference/geom_bar.html) counts; [`geom_col()`](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/reference/geom_bar.html) uses your values; position changes the question.
4. **Model plots are conditional claims.** Predictions, slopes, and comparisons answer different questions; name the interval and the scale.
5. **Composition and export are part of the argument.** A figure that cannot be read at final size, or by a colour-blind reader, is not finished.

:::

::: {.column width="45%"}
::: {.callout-important}
### The model is not the plot

A plot of predictions is a view of a model, not the model itself. Show the data, the fitted relation, and the uncertainty — and say which interval the band represents.
:::

**Next steps**

- Read the [ggplot2 book](https://ggplot2-book.org/) chapters on scales, guides, and extensions.
- Try [`ggdist`](https://mjskay.github.io/ggdist/), [`patchwork`](https://patchwork.data-imaginist.com/), [`ggeffects`](https://strengejacke.github.io/ggeffects/), and [`marginaleffects`](https://marginaleffects.com/) on your own data.
- Audit one figure from your last paper with the accessibility checklist.
- Bring a model or a composite figure to the next RDM session.

:::

:::

::: {.notes}
The advanced deck ends where publication begins. The grammar is still the transferable skill; the new material is about controlling the mapping, representing a model, and assembling a figure that survives review.
:::
